articles.title: The Division 2 Review - IGN
articles.summary: By genre standards, this shared-world shooter has launched fully loaded.
articles.body:
More than any freshly launched shared-world shooter to date, Tom Clancy’s The Division 2 presents a polished, well-thought-out initial progression path with at least some gas left in the tank after the fact. Its great gunplay, worthwhile loot, and beautiful world brimming with reasons to explore it kept me engrossed for the vast majority of my 60 hours of playtime. After all that momentum, it was a bit of a shock to the system to discover that the difficult endgame content that I had been looking forward to in World Tier 4 didn’t produce any worthwhile rewards or meaningful new mechanical challenges. The Dark Zone, too, was far less interesting that I had hoped it would be. But the good news is that these late-game shortcomings don’t take away from the great journey that I underwent to reach them. The Division 2 gets so much more right than it does wrong.

Things in The Division 2 seem to pick up right where the original post-pandemic story left off in terms of both plotline and cover-based shooting, but it quickly becomes clear that many aspects of the gameplay have improved in meaningful ways. Gunplay is impactful – enemies react to being shot sooner and die faster, and the world is teeming with enticing reasons to explore it. There are chests and collectibles around every corner, and this generous distribution of loot goes a long way in the context of The Division 2’s phenomenally well-realized recreation of Washington D.C. The capital is painstakingly populated with a fanatical amount of detail and boasts much more in the way of environmental variance than the first game’s depiction of New York City. The series’ familiar and predictable urban grid gives way to lush, open vistas and iconic monuments overtaken by vines. It all comes together to provide a space that makes it okay to stop and smell the roses, I never regretted indulging my inner explorer.

All main-mission and stronghold bosses, on all difficulty levels, just seem to be normal enemy archetypes with more health. This deprives the PvE encounters of sorely needed stand-out moments and mechanical intricacy. The only one who (barely) breaks this rule is Diesel, from the District Union Arena, who briefly takes control of a turret on a stationary armored car but then just turns out to be another armor-clad Hyena machine gunner. Bespoke boss mechanics are a staple of the shared-world shooter and action RPG genres, so I was expecting to see some more elaborate encounters, especially in The Division 2’s strongholds , but came up empty. The good news is that enemy variety elsewhere is significantly better than the first game.

The expected assortment of enemy archetypes, like rushers, snipers, and engineers are all here, but some factions like the Mad Max-esque “Outcasts” take some entertaining creative liberties with these roles. Their rusher is a suicide bomber, their engineer controls a Battle Bot, and their heavy tries to crush your skull with a giant hammer. Most adversaries can spawn as more a difficult version of their basic role, and get a correspondingly colored health bar to indicate who can take a few more hits. A sneaky improvement over the first game is that harder content doesn’t strictly mean more high-health enemies, even challenge-difficulty strongholds provide you with plenty of “red bar” fodder to cut your teeth on. These lowly grunts may melt quickly, but they pack a punch and can spell trouble if they get behind you. As a result of these factors, combat remained demanding and fun, if a little predictable, throughout my 60 hours with The Division 2.

There were a handful of times when encounters felt a little spongy, but this was usually a result of attempting content I wasn’t quite ready for in terms of gear score, which is the primary measurement that The Division 2 uses to determine your power after level 30. For the most part, I found even bosses died reasonably quickly and that time-to-kill was a non-issue, which again, is an achievement for a stat-based shooter. The handful of baddies that can take a beating are generally covered in bulky, hard-to-miss kevlar that breaks off as you shoot it, making their superhuman durability more believable. It’s easy to wince at the idea of an intentionally spongy foe in The Division 2, but these tanky brutes move at a snail's pace and always added a welcome bit of variety.

Tinkering with your build is easy and intuitive thanks to a well-detailed stat summary and DPS meters in the form of the firing range. I had loads of fun eeking out every last drop of damage from brand set bonuses, weapon attachments, attributes, and talents. This welcome clarity does shine a harsh light on The Division 2’s weapon balance, or lack thereof. LMGs, assault rifles, and sniper rifles all perform as you’d expect them to, but shotguns especially felt weak by comparison even after tweaking my build.

While gunplay is much improved in The Division 2, the abilities we get to use still feel clunky and ineffective. Deployed turrets get destroyed almost instantly, and anything that requires a second activation, like the Bomber Drone, took too long to set up relative to the middling damage it delivered in my initial playthrough. The handful of skills that did feel useful like the healing Chem Launcher, Reviver Hive, and Ballistic shield were already serving their purpose at their base power and therefore didn’t provoke much exploration into a “skill power” build. Even if I wanted to, the required skill power to equip an ability mod was always way above my means and therefore the whole concept was a bit a non-starter. Specializations, on the other hand, do offer phenomenally fun-to-use signature weapons up front, as well as useful bonuses like different grenades, skills, and passive effects as you level them up.

There are a lot of excellent activities and progression that await you after the critical path, at least for a while anyway. You’ll unlock powerful signature weapons, be introduced to dynamic world systems like the priority target networks, and even go up against a new faction that’s introduced after the campaign in “invaded” versions of previously completed missions. Item levels are replaced by gear score, and for a brief time between World Tiers 1 and 4, everything works beautifully thanks to the new, rewarding content. But this “endgame” is really more of an epilogue due to its brevity – it only lasts about six hours. Once you’ve completed the invaded missions and progress to World Tier 4 you lose the ability to replay them and instead gain access to challenging variants of missions you’ve already played with no mechanical difference from the main campaign and rewards that stagnate very quickly. This is the real endgame, and it’s where things start to fall apart for The Division 2’s intuitive and well-communicated progression loop.

It’s easy to find high-end items in World Tier 4 through simplistic means like looting chests, killing enemies, and completing normal-difficulty activities and missions. Before you know it, you’ll reach the gear score cap of 450 and be inundated with hundreds of randomly generated high-end items that aren’t clearly better than what you’ve already got. This is where things get a little confusing because of the unintuitive and inconsistent ways in which The Division 2 allows you to circumvent this soft cap and continue making progress. You can get hold of items with a gear score higher than 450 by opening proficiency caches awarded for gaining normal experience, Dark Zone experience, or by winning matches of The Division 2’s organized PvP mode called Conflict, plus a few other ways. I was shocked when all of the other places where I would expect these better-than-average rewards to come from, including daily and weekly projects as well as challenge-difficulty strongholds, missions, and high-value bounties only gave me more of the same 450 gear level items I could obtain from much easier sources. The result is that The Division 2’s once broad and replayable content is arbitrarily cut into two halves – one that advances your gear score, and one that does not.

The good news here is that gear score isn’t nearly as important as itemization when it comes to effective power. Progression after 450 takes the form of identifying the most advantageous talents, attributes, and brand sets (which are basically mini set bonuses) and distilling your hoard of hundreds of high-end items down the absolute best one percent. And mercifully, there are still a lot other things to do in the interim between now and the upcoming Tidal Basin update, which Ubisoft says will “soon” introduce a new stronghold, World Tier 5 , gear sets, heroic difficulty, weekly invasions, and increase the gear score cap.

Capture points, which are fun the whole game through, become even more enjoyable when dynamic difficulty ranks are introduced. Completing activities in the surrounding area increases the difficulty of the closest capture point, which at ranks three and above awards essential weapon attachments. There are also an enormity of fun and fruitful Easter egg hunts that I can see taking up the majority of my time in between now and the first update. Cryptic puzzles result in the appearance of mysterious enemies who drop coveted masks, just about every main mission has a hidden backpack charm, and two of the best currently known exotic weapons are the end result of a hunt for unique crafting components. Annoyingly, crafting the Liberty exotic is contingent on a specific high-end weapon dropping to complete the recipe, but I suppose this isn’t that unforgiving as far as ARPG grinds go.

So what about playing the Dark Zone for the fun of it? Well, it’s a less attractive and dynamic space without the consequence of potentially losing or stealing items that you care about, but it’s fun enough on its own. Combat in both the normal and occupied Dark Zones is much more intuitive than in the original The Division ’s version, thanks largely to a faster time-to-kill. Killing a fellow agent in the non-occupied Dark Zone will result in you and your squad going rogue, an action that – if you repeat it enough – will trigger a map-wide manhunt where everybody’s out for your blood. You can hack away your bounty at manhunt stations or, if you’re so bold, double down and increase your manhunt tier. Completing the ultimate Dark Zone achievement of a tier 1 manhunt doesn’t offer any exclusive cosmetics on its own, which seems like a missed opportunity for getting people to chase bragging rights, but it does award gear score 250 items. That’s right: complete arguably the toughest achievement The Division 2 has to offer and you’ll be the proud owner of an item that’s a full 200 gear score less than that you’ll find off a run-of-the-mill red-bar goon. And, in my experience, none of these items offered any kind of Dark Zone-exclusive perks or talents. The rewards for successful bartering with the illusive Thieves’ Den vendor are much the same.

The only risk-reward dynamic that’s intact in the Dark Zone at endgame is experience gain and loss, but even that loses its potency eventually. Killing another player in the anything-goes occupied Dark Zone grants a large experience bonus, but dying is catastrophic, at times resulting in the spoils from a whole Dark Zone level being lost. Dying in the normal Dark Zone isn’t as brutal, but you will lose a fair chunk if you’ve “gone rogue” by scoring a kill on a non-rogue agent or by performing a handful of shady deeds like stealing chests and Dark Zone drops. I went “disavowed” rogue a lot because I’m kind of a jerk like that, but I wouldn’t recommend it if you’re just trying to hit max rank in the Dark Zone as the risks are not worth the reward. Once you reach rank 50 you’ll be rewarded with a proficiency cache for over-leveling, but you seem to lose the ability to rank down which makes the space that much less daunting. If nothing else, it is a good place to farm huge amounts of 450 items.

To be clear, my issue with The Division 2’s endgame is not that it is too short or lacking in content, but rather that it fails to effectively direct you to the best and most replayable content that’s already there with worthwhile rewards. It’s also disappointing that the challenge difficulty option which is kept from you until the absolute endgame offers nothing new in the way of mechanical variance.

articles.title: It’s a spooky season miracle — Alien: Isolation is getting a sequel
articles.summary: On the 10th anniversary of the release of Alien: Isolation, the developers at Creative Assembly have announced that they are working on a sequel.
articles.body: To celebrate the 10th anniversary of the release of Alien: Isolation, the developers at Creative Assembly have announced they’re working on a sequel. “We have heard your distress calls loud and clear,” wrote Al Hope, creative director at Creative Assembly. “I’m delighted to confirm, on behalf of the team, that a sequel to Alien: Isolation is in early development.” Alien: Isolation released in 2014 to rave reviews, marking it as one of the best video game adaptations from the Alien franchise. It stars Amanda Ripley, daughter of Ellen “get away from her, you bitch” Ripley as she attempts to discover what happened to her mother 15 years after the events of the first Alien movie. Part of the reason for the game’s success is because it taps into the anxiety of fear. Rather than confront the xenomorphs directly, Alien: Isolation requires that Amanda complete her objectives while trying to avoid and escape them, arming her with franchise staple tools like motion trackers and flamethrowers. The Alien franchise has been on an upswing lately. The latest movie, Alien: Romulus, was regarded as a decent return to the series’ claustrophobic survival horror roots after the wild creative swings that were taken by Prometheus and Alien: Covenant. There’s also an Alien TV show set to debut next year, helmed by Fargo showrunner Noah Hawley.

articles.title: The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion – I Spent 44 Hours in 4 Days Playing It in Bethesda's Basement
articles.summary: The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion was arguably the defining moment of the first months of the HD Era and a true killer app for the Xbox 360 – you had to buy the console so you wouldn’t miss out on this game. And if you’ve made it this far, I’ll bet you’ve got lots of great memories of this one too. Here’s hoping that The Elder Scrolls 6 can recapture at least some of that magic.
articles.body:
I imagine the Xbox stories I’ve been sharing on IGN recently in the run-up to the brand’s 25th anniversary probably seem a little ridiculous or even a bit crazy now – like how I got to be one of the first people to ever play through Halo 2 while playing in a storage closet at Bungie – but I promise you, it was all pretty normal back then. Today I have another one of those stories for you, and it’s one of my favorite gaming memories of all time. It’s about The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion.

If you were a gamer back when the Xbox 360 first came out, you’ll remember how big a deal it was that the Xbox 360 was the first console of the “HD Era,” as the entire history of video games up to that point (at least on the console side – respect to my fellow PC gamers who’d been 1024x768’ing it for years by then). Finally we were moving from 640x480 (interlaced, to boot) to 1280x720. It sounds quaint now, but it was a huge leap at the time. The 360 had gotten off to a fast start in November of 2005 thanks to the likes of Call of Duty 2, Project Gotham Racing 3, and then a couple months later, the jaw-dropping Fight Night Round 3. But there was one game we were all anticipating far more than any other in the 360’s first months: The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion. It was supposed to be a day-one launch title for the new Xbox, but it got delayed .

I was personally and professionally so excited for this game, as it seemed like my ultimate medieval fantasy RPG come to life. And so I’d spearheaded Official Xbox Magazine’s coverage throughout 2005; I think I made at least two trips out to Bethesda Game Studios in Maryland that year as excitement for the game and the console built. The studio had already won a lot of console-gamer fans through its 2002 original Xbox port of The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind, but this time, Oblivion was readied as a day-one Xbox 360 game, simultaneous to its PC launch. And what I had seen on those trips – translated into feature stories in OXM – had only fueled my hype even more. The stunning graphics, the incredible music, the “living” NPCs who had daily routines they’d go through whether you were around or not – it all felt like it was coalescing into something truly special.

So when it finally came time to review Oblivion, OXM was once again able to secure the exclusive review. Combined with the lead times necessitated by magazine publishing schedules, it meant that I found myself back at Bethesda in January of 2006 to review Oblivion, which shipped in March. Everyone knew it’d be a big game – Morrowind most certainly was – and so the plan was to spend four days at Bethesda and play as much as I possibly could. When I arrived at the studio, I was brought down to the basement floor, I said hello (again) to Todd Howard, and then I was escorted into a glass-walled conference room. There I had a giant TV at one end of the room, my chair and an Xbox 360 dev kit at the other end of the room, and a controller on the table. And then everyone else left.

My mission was to get as many hours under my belt as I could before heading home to write the review for the magazine. My hotel was literally next door to Bethesda’s office, so I wouldn’t even have to spend time getting to and from the studio. Food was ordered in for me, and I took short breaks and ate right in the conference room. It was just me and the archer/thief I’d created for 44 hours over four days. Yes, I spent roughly 11 hours per day living in Cyrodiil without having to think about anything else: no other work, no other responsibilities. It was amazing, and one of the best gaming experiences of my life.

I explored, I fought, I snuck, I stole, I joined the Dark Brotherhood, I closed a whole bunch of Oblivion Gates, and yes, I made sure to complete the main story questline. I even found, tamed, and rode a unicorn in the forest. The worst part of all of this was twofold: one, having to stop. And two, having to start over once the final retail copies of the game arrived. But as a testament to how incredible that game was (and thankfully still is, thanks to last year’s great remaster ), I put another 125-plus hours into it at home in March, soaking in every DLC and expansion that dropped after launch. (I gave Oblivion a 9.5 out of 10 in OXM, if you’re curious.)

The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion was arguably the defining moment of the first months of the HD Era and a true killer app for the Xbox 360 – you had to buy the console so you wouldn’t miss out on this game. And if you’ve made it this far, I’ll bet you’ve got lots of great memories of this one too. Here’s hoping that The Elder Scrolls 6 can recapture at least some of that magic.

Ryan McCaffrey is IGN's executive editor of previews and host of IGN's weekly Xbox show, Podcast Unlocked , and a co-host of Next-Gen Console Watch . He's a North Jersey guy, so it's "Taylor ham," not "pork roll." Debate it with him on Twitter at @DMC_Ryan .

articles.title: The Chronicles of Riddick: Escape from Butcher Bay Remains One of the Most Underrated Games Ever
articles.summary: The Chronicles of Riddick: Escape from Butcher Bay didn’t just break the licensed-game curse, it was a bona fide Game of the Year contender on Xbox that year (it was won by a little game called Halo 2 that released in November of that year).
articles.body:
This is an IGN opinion piece from Ryan McCaffrey, who worked at Official Xbox Magazine from 2002-2012 during the original Xbox and Xbox 360 era before joining IGN, where he remains “the Xbox guy.” In the run-up to Xbox’s 25th anniversary, he’ll be sharing his memories from the platform’s first quarter-century.

When I worked at Official Xbox Magazine, the first thing you came upon when you entered our area of the office was our demo station. There sat a small couch and our biggest TV, a behemoth 36-inch CRT that could display at 480p – meaning, the same resolution as every other console game, but without the interlacing, thus creating a crisper image. Because when developers came through to show us their in-progress games, we wanted them to look their best. I was never more grateful for that gigantic 480p TV than when a then-unknown (at least to me) Swedish developer named Starbreeze came by to show off the licensed game they were working on: The Chronicles of Riddick: Escape From Butcher Bay.

“Whatever,” I thought. “It’ll just be a cheap movie cash-in.” And then I actually saw it and my jaw hit the floor.

Funny enough, the first thing that made my eyes go wide wasn’t even the game itself – though that would happen in a few more moments. No, I and the rest of the OXM team were transfixed by Riddick’s front-end menu screen . See, it was a normal-mapped 3D cube whose letters erupted from and receded into the shiny, beautifully textured cube when you moved from one selection to the next. Normal-mapping was a new graphics toy then; we’d really not seen it before on a console. But the Xbox was fully capable, and other games on the console besides Riddick went on to put it to good use.

But back to Riddick. The Starbreeze team proceeded to show us a first-person prison-break game with insane lighting, RPG-like dialogue with myriad NPCs, an awesome hide-in-the-shadows stealth system built around the titular anti-hero’s “eye shine” that allows him to see in the dark, some horror elements, and a reasonable bit of first-person shooting as well. And when we got our hands on the full game ahead of its release in June 2004, they’d successfully built an entire game this good. It had the graphics, the audio, the atmosphere, the story, the gameplay. It had everything.

Riddick didn’t just break the licensed-game curse, it was a bona fide Game of the Year contender on Xbox that year (it was won by a little game called Halo 2 that released in November of that year). And if you’re wondering, “Wait, what licensed-game curse?” For you younger readers, video games based on licensed properties were almost universally, take-it-to-the-bank guaranteed to be terrible. This wasn’t for a lack of effort by game developers. Rather, it was game publishers who thought they could spend the least amount of money possible – be it on talent, length of development cycle, or both – and it wouldn’t matter because people would buy the game anyway because of the licensed property adorning the front of the box. And I suppose they must’ve been right on some level, because for years, good (let alone great) licensed games were the exception, not the rule.

Riddick was the first crack in that dam that has since broken (see also: Batman: Arkham Asylum). It’s certainly not that every licensed game is good now, but games like Riddick and Batman: Arkham have finally shown publishers that if they invest in top talent and give them sufficient resources, that they can make way, way more money than just going for the cheap cash grab.

Also, Vin Diesel himself deserves some credit as well, even if Starbreeze gets the lion’s share of it. Diesel was (and presumably still is) a big gamer, and he took an active role in the project through his Tigon Studios development team that assisted on Escape from Butcher Bay. Diesel didn’t want his character headlining a crappy game any more than players did, and in partnering with the then-relatively-unknown Starbreeze, he helped make sure that Richard B. Riddick wouldn’t suffer the same fate so many other characters making the transition from the big screen to the game-console screen did.

As phenomenal as Escape from Butcher Bay was, it’s arguably still pretty criminally underrated. If you never got a chance to play it, it’s not too late. Sure, the graphics won’t blow you away (or even impress you) in 2026, but the gameplay holds up pretty well.

articles.title: Rainbow Six Tactics Features Optional Permadeath, Ironman Mode
articles.summary: Ubisoft just announced Rainbow Six Tactics, a single-player turn-based tactics game starring 15 fan-favorite Operators from the popular long-running multiplayer first-person shooter Rainbow Six Siege. I had the chance to talk to Tactics game director Martial Potron about creating the first single-player Rainbow Six game since Rainbow Six Vegas 2 in 2008, including his thoughts on other franchises that have successfully pivoted genres, the importance of being a tactics game first, and more.
articles.body:
Ubisoft just announced Rainbow Six Tactics, a single-player turn-based tactics game starring 15 fan-favorite Operators from the popular long-running multiplayer first-person shooter Rainbow Six Siege. I had the chance to talk to Tactics game director Martial Potron about creating the first single-player Rainbow Six game since Rainbow Six Vegas 2 in 2008, including his thoughts on other franchises that have successfully pivoted genres, the importance of being a tactics game first, and more.

First, on that tactics-genre staple of permadeath, Potron said, "We know it’s a must-have for tactical fans. R6T features optional permadeath, as well as an Ironman mode. In practical terms, Operators who are too severely injured can be permanently unavailable for the rest of the campaign. Players can enable it at any difficulty level, so they can experience the added tension of risking to lose an operator on an easier setting. It dramatically changes the way you play, because operators are unique and not replaceable. Losing a favourite or highly progressed Operator forces players to adapt their strategy and rethink squad composition."

I reference Gears Tactics as another big action franchise that made a pretty successful pivot to tactics, and Potron didn't do the usual move of not mentioning anyone else's game by name, and offered this when I asked about lessons learned from other games that have dipped their toes in the tactics waters: "The key lesson is that the game must first succeed on its own terms," he said. "Tactical-game fans have very high expectations, so R6 Tactics has to stand as a strong tactics game before it can succeed as a Rainbow Six game. Our franchise competitors that ventured into the tactics genre succeeded because they combined strong franchises with excellent design, canon storytelling, and production values.

"The second lesson is that a genre shift works best when it translates the franchise identity rather than simply reskinning another formula. Gears Tactics, for example, adapted executions and emergence holes to recreate the pace and aggression of Gears. Despite being turn-based, the game still felt unmistakably like Gears.

"Regarding Rainbow Six, one might think it’ll be a challenge to adapt a shooter, where much of the fun comes from aiming, reacting, and executing. But the Rainbow Franchise fortunately already have this ideal of being the Smart Shooter, where thinking before acting is paramount. Our job is not to impose tactics on Rainbow Six, but to express the tactical thinking that has always defined it through a new genre. So for us, the transition was smooth as all the elements were already there. Shooting, reconnaissance, breaching, gadgets, and coordination cannot feel like generic tactics mechanics; each decision must feel specifically like Rainbow Six."

Potron also told me that there are lots of references to the entire series in Tactics. "The planning phase of the original Rainbow Six was a key inspiration for one of our main features: the Breach. Players can coordinate an assault on a heavily defended location by choosing entry points (doors, windows, or any destructible wall); assigning operators to them, and synchronizing explosives, grenades, and shots to neutralize as many enemies as possible before turn-based combat resumes. It’s our modern take on this feature of the early games.

"There are other nods throughout Tactics as well. At the start of missions, players choose insertion points that shape their approach and the risks they take. On the narrative side, rebuilding Rainbow after its destruction in Siege’s Year 10 also allowed us to reconnect with the wider story of the franchise, including Paul Bishop from Rainbow Six Vegas 2. We worked closely with the Rainbow team in Montreal to make sure everything was properly tied together. So yes, we drew from the entire history of Rainbow Six, from the earliest games to Vegas and Siege, to create both gameplay and narrative touchstones."

Finally, I asked Potron what from Siege translated well to a tactics game and what required clever reintrpretation. He went right to one of Siege's signature features for the former: destruction. "In most tactical games, players must flank, cover and work with existing lines of sight. Here, they can create new paths and firing angles by destroying walls and covers. But enemies can do the same, which means no position is completely safe. This fundamentally changes how players approach the battlefield.

"Breach planning, an iconic feature of classic Rainbow Six, was also at the heart of our reflection. Players select entry points, coordinate four operators, assign grenades and abilities, and prioritize dangerous targets. A single plan can contain up to twelve decisions before the player presses “Execute.” Balancing that depth with accessibility—and then turning all those synchronized actions into one clear, cinematic sequence—required considerable iteration.

"The biggest reinterpretation was translating Siege’s uncertainty into a turn-based format. In Siege, danger often comes from not knowing what is behind a wall, a corner, or a barricade. In R6 Tactics, our precise & dynamic fog-of-war system recreates that tension. Careful scouting and drones become essential before breaching. The key was balancing tension with fairness, so hidden threats remain dangerous without becoming frustrating."

Rainbow Six Tactics is due out next year for PC, PS5, and Xbox Series X|S.

While not the most expensive LEGO set or the model with the most bricks , the Executor's vast length will break a fresh record for the toy firm in terms of its length. At more than 136 cm long, this 6,130-piece Ultimate Collector Series model is one you'd need a very deep Dagobah swamp to hide in.

Priced at a stonking $799.99 (£649.99), the set will become available on October 4, or via early access to LEGO Insiders from October 1. And if you need to measure up your home to find out if it'll fit, the set's dimensions will be 7.5 inches (20 cm) in height, 53.5 inches (136 cm) in length and 20 inches (50 cm) in width. Finally, it'll weigh just over 11 lbs / 5 kg.

LEGO Star Wars Executor Super Star Destroyer Images

Which ship is the Executor? This is the super sleek, supersized Star Destroyer that Darth Vader uses as his flagship in The Empire Strikes Back and Return of the Jedi. Present at the Battle of Hoth and Battle of Endor, this ship is also the setting for Vader's meeting with various bounty hunters, included here as minifigures.

In Star Wars lore, the actual Executor was over 19 km in length — roughly the size of Manhatten. The Executor was only finally beaten when a brave Rebel pilot crashed into its command bridge during the battle around Endor's moon, disabling the gargantuan vessel's shields and sinking it into the second Death Star (another Empire design flaw). It was apparently crewed by a vast army in the hundreds of thousands — but best not think too much about that.

The LEGO Star Wars Executor set will weigh in at a hefty 6,130 pieces and include a mini build of the ship's bridge. Minifigures include Darth Vader, Boba Fett, Dengar, Bossk, IG-88, 4-LOM, and Zuckuss. LEGO Insiders will be eligible for a Gift With Purchase (while stocks last) of a buildable recreation of Darth Vader's Lightsaber.

It's been a busy day for LEGO news, with the full reveal of the company's Super Mario minifigure set range . Keen for something even larger? We have a guide to the biggest LEGO sets you can buy in 2026 .

articles.title: Guinean President Mamadi Doumbouya dismisses 173 soldiers for desertion
articles.summary: It is thought to be part of efforts to consolidate the former coup leader's control.
articles.body:
Guinea's President Mamadi Doumbouya, 41, has dismissed more than 170 soldiers for "desertion", including a colonel who helped him seize power in a coup in 2021.

Col Michel Lamah was a member of the Special Forces Group (GFS), the elite army unit which Doumbouya once commanded.

When he overthrew President Alpha Condé, Doumbouya said he would not seek election and would hand over to civilian rule. He went on to renege on that promise and stood in December's election - which he won with a landslide.

The dismissals, announced in a decree on state television, are thought to be part of ongoing efforts by the president to consolidate his control and prevent potential challenges to his leadership.

Those in the firing line came from various branches of the military. No details were given about the circumstances of the alleged desertions of the 173 military personnel when Gen Amara Camara, the president's spokesman, read out the decree on Monday.

From camouflage to tracksuits - Guinea's junta leader becomes civilian president

Col Lamah caught public attention during the September 2021 coup when he was photographed in a vehicle carrying deposed President Condé.

Troops had stormed the presidential palace and arrested Condé, who had been re-elected the year before for a controversial third term in office amid violent protests.

Since the coup, the West African nation has seen a crackdown on many civil liberties.

Media outlets have been shut down, protests have been banned and some political parties have been suspended, while activists and opposition figures have been arrested or exiled.

Two of Guinea's biggest opposition parties - RPG Arc en Ciel and UFDG - were excluded from last year's election, which saw the former junta leader win 87% of the vote.

Over the last five years, Doumbouya has been focused on trying to turn Guinea, which is rich in mineral resources, from a supplier of raw materials to more of an industrial processing hub.

articles.title: Rupert Grint Returning as Ron Weasley for Harry Potter and The Cursed Child on Broadway
articles.summary: Harry Potter movie star Rupert Grint will reprise his character of Ron Weasley next year, as he joins the Broadway cast of Harry Potter and the Cursed Child.
articles.body:
Harry Potter movie star Rupert Grint will reprise his character of Ron Weasley next year, as he joins the Broadway cast of Harry Potter and the Cursed Child .

Grint is the second Harry Potter movie cast member to return to their childhood role for Cursed Child, the official J.K. Rowling-penned play that picks up the series' story years later, as Harry and Ron's children attend Hogwarts.

Last year, Draco Malfoy actor Tom Felton returned as his fan-favorite Slytherin, supercharging interest in the Broadway production. Now, it seems like the play's producers are keen to pull off the same stunt again, with Grint also the right age to play Ron as a young father.

Harry Potter HBO TV Series Cast and Characters: Who's Confirmed for the Reboot?

"Ron Weasley has been a part of me since I was 11 years old and I can't wait to meet him again in this stage of life," Weasley said, via The Hollywood Reporter . "There is something so full-circle and so special about stepping back into Ron's shoes now when we are both fathers; it is somehow both very familiar and completely new. And the joy of being back on Broadway, this time in a role that defined so much of my life is truly exciting."

Grint will begin his stint back as Ron on February 2, 2027, initially for a 17-week run until May 30. However, this does mean his time in the play's company will sadly not overlap with Felton, whose much-extended time in the cast finally ends on January 3, 2027.

While Grint is still best known for his Harry Potter role, the actor has continued to appear in a string of TV and film projects, such as Apple TV horror series Servant, M. Night Shyamalan movie Knock at the Cabin, and this year's upcoming Johnny Depp-starring Ebenezer , in which he plays Bob Cratchit.

"In joining our extraordinary company onstage at the Lyric Theatre in New York City, Rupert is not simply revisiting a role from his past," producers Sonia Friedman and Colin Callender said in a statement. "He is continuing a journey he began as a child and carrying it forward with all the life and experience he has gained since filming concluded, including a career that has taken him from film to television to acclaimed stage work on both Broadway and the West End. His return creates a powerful bridge between the story audiences first fell in love with and the story of family, legacy and the passage of time that Harry Potter and the Cursed Child carries forward."

Of course, a fresh generation of young actors will soon take on the roles of Harry, Ron and Draco in HBO's Harry Potter TV series reboot . Set to launch this Christmas, the show will adapt the franchise over the course of the next decade.

articles.title: Crazy Taxi: World Tour Has the YA YA YA YA YAs but Stumbles With the “World” Part of World Tour – Gamescom 2026
articles.summary: Crazy Taxi: World Tour is an almost refreshingly uncomplicated palette cleanser free of skill trees, crafting systems, and the other chaff that seems to be in every game you play nowadays. I just hope they manage to make the levels worthy of the “World Tour” moniker this new ride has.
articles.body:
The core gameplay hits that nostalgic Crazy Taxi note.

There's not enough of the specific around-the-world locations built into the maps.

One of the defining games of Sega’s Dreamcast back in the day was the arcade driving game, Crazy Taxi, first released more than a quarter of a century ago. With its fantastic soundtrack and its frenetic driving, it is about as quintessential “early 2000s” as you can get with a video game, and it has been 12 years since the last game released bearing the Crazy Taxi banner and double that since the last console release. Recently, Sega had us out to get a little hands-on time with the brand new entry, Crazy Taxi: World Tour, that was first announced back at Summer Game Fest earlier this summer. With The Offspring screaming YA YA YA YA YA at me, I slammed down the pedal and off I went to pick up my first passenger, mostly happy with what’s here but wishing it did more to put the “world” in “World Tour.”

Revealed just recently at GamesCom was a brand new level making its debut: Germany. The new level has most of those ingredients that you would want from a fast-paced arcade game like Crazy Taxi. I was dropped onto the tarmac of a large airport, a great place to get used to how the cab controls and feels while pulling off some sick donuts. The large size of the hazards also made them easy to avoid… most of the time. Once I was done taking passengers from one side of the airport to the other, it was off to explore the rest of the level.

The region is divided into five areas: the airport where you start, the City, the Walled City, the Mountains, and the Autobahn that connects them all. I’m not entirely sure about how an airport screams “Germany”, but the other areas, especially the city areas, did give off at least a little bit of a Deutschland vibe. One of the niftier additions to World Tour, though, was being able to at any hop into a menu and change the time of day, with my options including being able to pick from morning, afternoon, evening, or night.

Outside of simple visual aesthetics, I didn’t really notice this time shift affecting the gameplay at all, be it the number of passengers that were out, the density of the traffic, or what odd jobs appeared. I also didn’t notice time passing naturally, but that could just be due to having so little time with World Tour. Hopefully in the final game, the sun will rise and set on its own as you drive around, because each time of day featured its own distinct beauty, and I wouldn’t mind the time of day impacting how the areas behaved. Regardless, driving around during the golden hour of evening or while surrounded by the lights of buildings at nighttime was pretty neat.

Speaking of driving, as it’s the pillar that the Crazy Taxi series is built upon,World Tour controlled really well, letting me pull off tight turns, sick boosts off ramps, and quick dodges around oncoming traffic. Acceleration felt right, and managing to utilize the fast break right on cue feels damn good. I’ve always gravitated more towards arcade racers than driving sims, especially those from the era that Crazy Taxi comes from. Where acceleration is fast, there are shortcuts sprinkled all over for you to discover, and mastering its movement and maps almost becomes an art form. I didn’t have enough time to really regain all my cabbie instincts, and my reaction times are a bit slower than when I was in my teens; it still seems to be on the right track to nail what I remember the old games not only feeling like, but hearing like, too.

The moment those first few chords of The Offspring started, though, it was like I hopped in the back seat of Axel’s taxi and was whisked away back to the early 2000s, where I just wanted to turn my brain off and zip around trying to beat my personal best records and listening to sweet tunes. It really makes me smile that the team understands just how closely linked Crazy Taxi is to the music. I associate the “All I want” and its signature YA YA YAs to Crazy Taxi just like I connect Tony Hawk with Goldfinger’s “Superman” track, and to hear it back in World Tour really helps tie it together.

But my time in fictional Germany wasn’t spent just vibing to late ‘90s skate punk and taking passengers to their destinations. Other activities, including various odd jobs and skill tests, were available to check out, giving me a little break when I wanted to take a rest from delivering passengers. These all required me to drive fast, of course, but were usually nice breaks from the typical getting from point A to point B.

During one of these jobs, I had the environmentally crucial task of driving into neatly stacked piles of nearby paper so that the worker in the backseat, equipped with a vacuum, could suck them all up. The one I probably had the most fun with, though, was where I had to slam on my brakes and send a guy in a wingsuit flying, trying to rack up the most distance. At least up until my demo crashed and I had to call it quits (but hey, it’s a pre-release build; it happens).

Crazy Taxi: World Tour - Gamescom 2026 Screenshots

The whole time I was zooming around picking up fares and boosting off ramps, and even though I was having a fun time doing it, there was a nagging thought in the back of my mind, like a bug buzzing around inside while you're driving – things just looked sort of, well, generic? While the cab itself looks pretty fly, the various other cars on the roads and especially the NPC passengers lacked detail or much personality. Largely coming off as something pulled off an asset store.

The fact that I was driving around what was supposedly Germany, outside of the map telling me, and colorful arched buildings (which, had I not been told, I would have just attributed as “generic European town” I would have just assumed it was a random place. I would love it if Sega leaned into the culture a bit more. Have the passengers speak with a German accent or have the occasional townsperson swap their shorts for some sick Lederhosen. I get that the vast majority of people don’t wander around like that anymore, but taxi drivers don’t have green flames bursting from their tires either. And I’m still trying to figure out what about the airport is supposed to make me feel like I’m in Germany, aside from the occasional sign in what I assume is German alongside the ones that are still in English. Why take me around the world if you aren’t going to represent the people as well as the scenery? This is a game where you drive a taxi; if I’m driving around in Germany, shouldn’t I be picking up German passengers, or at least folks that sound like they’re German?

Still, even in this early state, as I was drifting and boosting around Germany, I settled into that peaceful, serene sort of state when I could see myself just doing it for hours. The whole loop, while simplistic, was just fun. There is a reason that the Crazy Taxi series is beloved by so many who grew up with it, calling for its return for so long. It has been a series I’ve always checked out from afar, and only occasionally getting behind the wheel myself, but I get it now.

Playing Crazy Taxi: World Tour, even briefly, was just that simple-yet-exciting sort of fun that arcade games excel at, that makes you want to just keep playing. An almost refreshingly uncomplicated palette cleanser free of skill trees, crafting systems, and the other chaff that seems to be in every game you play nowadays. I just hope they manage to make the levels worthy of the “World Tour” moniker this new ride has.

articles.title: Xbox Is Letting Players Digitize Their Physical Games, Starting Next Week for Select Users
articles.summary: Xbox's new disc-to-digital feature is launching imminently, allowing users to add physical copies of games to their digital library.
articles.body:
Xbox's new disc-to-digital feature is launching imminently, allowing users to add physical copies of games to their digital library.

The new feature will roll out to Xbox Insiders starting on August 31 before making its way to everyone at an unknown future date. This new initiative leaked earlier this summer and will be a way to allow players to put their Xbox One and Xbox Series X discs into their console and get a fully usable digital version.

Your discs will also remain playable, but if you give the game to someone else and they insert that copy into their console, you will lose access to your digital license as well. It's not only great for the sake of convenience, but perhaps more notably, it also enables you to stream the game through the cloud or access it on other devices via Xbox Play Anywhere if the game supports those features.

That means you don't have to have the game installed at all, and you can play it on PC, the ROG Ally, or even your mobile devices. Unfortunately, Microsoft made no mention of this feature being supported with original Xbox or Xbox 360 games, so don't expect those right now. Additionally, not every game will be supported off the bat. However, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma has said the company will support thousands of games when this feature launches, with more added over time. Will that eventually encompass Xbox 360 titles? It's hard to say.

"Your physical game library is more than a collection of discs," said Sharma . "It holds years of memories and stories worth preserving. Starting next week, Xbox Insiders can unlock a digital entitlement for supported physical games. We’ll start with thousands of titles and add more as we can."

Some have speculated that this move is happening to create a smooth transition between this generation and the next Xbox, which may be a digital-only device. Microsoft has yet to confirm such a thing, but given PlayStation won't support discs starting in 2028 , physical gaming media may be less of a standard next-gen. Regardless, this is a great feature that will definitely offer a lot of benefits to those who enjoy physical media.

Cade Onder is a freelancer for IGN's news team. He covers all things entertainment, including gaming, film, and more. You can find him on Twitter @Cade_Onder.

articles.title: Xbox boss 'thinking about affordability' of next-gen console
articles.summary: In an exclusive interview with the BBC, Asha Sharma also discusses giving gamers digital versions of games they own.
articles.body:
Xbox chief executive Asha Sharma says the gaming giant needs to be "thinking about" affordability for its next-generation console, amid a "crisis" in computing prices.

In an interview with the BBC, she said rising hardware costs partly driven by AI spending mean firms need to find ways to make gaming affordable.

She also revealed gamers will soon be able to get digital versions of many of the physical games they currently own, potentially meaning their old games can be played on future Xbox consoles without having to put a disc in a drive.

"I know players love physical media, and I know there's a lot of benefits in digital media, and I want to make sure people have a choice," Sharma said.

Currently, digital games can be downloaded online and played across Xbox consoles or PCs.

But some players prefer discs, with one of the main benefits being they can be bought and sold second-hand.

The topic has proven controversial, with Sony announcing new PlayStation games will no longer be released on discs from January 2028 , and the hotly-anticipated Grand Theft Auto VI similarly launching without a physical disc .

"There are stacks of games on everybody's shelves," Sharma said.

"We're announcing the ability for players for 1,000 titles with physical discs to be able to have a digital entitlement."

If a disc is sold second-hand, the digital rights would transfer over to the new owner.

Players will be able to access the feature by inserting one of the supported games into their Xbox console. And Sharma hinted it meant gamers would be able to play their old titles on future hardware.

"We've long pioneered backwards compatibility and so you'll continue to see that as we go forward in the generations," she said.

But she would not reveal whether Xbox's next-generation console - currently codenamed Project Helix - will have a disc drive at all.

"This next generation, we have to be thinking about efficiency and affordability alongside performance," she added.

For the first time in the history of gaming, consoles across the board have seen price hikes years after they came out.

This is partly due to component costs such as Ram skyrocketing in price as AI companies buy up all the parts for their data centres.

"As an industry, we're in the middle of 'Rampocalypse' ," Sharma said.

"All of the industry needs to start to innovate on affordability and efficiency. That is something that we have not had to do [previously].

"But with the crisis that's currently happening in hardware and components , it is absolutely something all of us need to be thinking about and innovating on and giving people more choice in terms of how they play their console and how they purchase their console."

Xbox is part of Microsoft, which is one of the companies ploughing the most money into AI infrastructure, which in turn puts the prices of hardware components up.

"AI is fundamentally changing a lot of things," Sharma said.

"Our job as Xbox, as we continue on in our next generation, is to take into consideration what's happening in the world and build the best experience for our players."

That meant, she said, for the next generation of consoles, Xbox had to think about "hardware efficiency in terms of how you use storage and memory, the kind of price per unit, the components, things like that".

Sharma has been in charge at Xbox for six months, having moved from Microsoft's AI division.

She has previously spoken of the need for " the most significant restructure in Xbox history " after years of underperformance.

Sharma told the BBC the "reset" was "to help ensure we are here for the next 25 years and we're continuing to serve our purpose".

In reality, that meant cutting thousands of jobs which "stunned" some of the affected workers .

She added: "We're in the middle of a new generation that wants to play in a different way, and new technology as well.

She admitted the next few years would be "challenging", but was taking a long-term view - with the prediction that "gaming is on the cusp of becoming the most important form of entertainment for the next century".

articles.title: Star Wars Zero Company PC Settings Guide
articles.body:
I’ve been an XCom fan for years, and while we haven’t got a new one in a while, Star Wars Zero Company seems like the perfect substitute. It’s in the Star Wars universe, which is awesome, and putting it in the middle of the Clone Wars makes it the perfect setting for a tactical game like this. And while I’ve been having a blast with it so far, it’s plagued with a lot of the same performance issues as Halo Campaign Evolved had about a month ago.

At the time of writing, my time with Zero Company has been a bit of a nightmare, filled with crashes and frame drops. I’m sure that, over time, the game will be patched to be a bit more stable, but right now, it doesn’t exactly play nice with low-to-mid-range hardware. I’ve even had some issues on an incredibly powerful RTX 5090 gaming PC .

While you can tune Zero Company to run a bit smoother most of the time, there are still issues with frame drops, particularly in cutscenes. Even if you get the game to run at a steady 60fps, there will be times when the game will run into hitches. One of the best ways around that is to have a PC with a decent processor.

When I tried to run the game on something like the Lenovo Legion Go 2, the CPU would be pinned at around 50–60% usage, while the GPU sat at 70–80%, which is just leaving performance on the table. Nvidia Reflex and AMD FSR Anti-Lag help a bit there, but most of the time you’re going to be limited by your CPU. Even on a desktop with a Ryzen 7 9850X3D and an RTX 5090, the game will occasionally spike CPU usage up to 50%, typically at the beginning of a mission.

Games using Unreal Engine 5 are hard to tune, but you can eke out some extra performance if you know where to cut. I’ll go through all the settings and what they change here, so you can tweak the game to your own specific PC. For example, if you have a weak CPU, you’re probably going to want to lower things like hidden objects and effect quality first.

Windowing Mode: This will change how the window is displayed when you’re playing the game. There are only three options. Fullscreen will make your computer only render the game, which could cause problems if you try to alt-tab. Borderless Window is what I like to call ‘fake fullscreen’ because it takes up your entire display while still rendering the Windows desktop beneath it. Then, Windowed mode just puts the game in a standard Window, where you can see the task bar. I’d choose Fullscreen if you’re on a single-monitor setup, and Borderless if you have multiple monitors or you alt-tab frequently.

Anti-Aliasing and Upscaling: Back in the day, there was a genuine debate over which type of upscaling folks should use, but these days, I’d just pick depending on who makes your graphics card. AMD users should use FSR, Nvidia users should use DLSS, and XeSS for Intel GPUs. This is a game where I’d recommend pretty much everyone to use some kind of upscaling to maximize performance.

Upscaling Quality: This changes the scale at which the game will be upscaled. Luckily, each GPU vendor uses the same scale, so I’d pick one depending on your native resolution. My rule of thumb is Performance for 4K, Balanced for 1440p, and Quality for 1080p.

Frame Generation: This uses AI to generate new frames and sandwiches them between natively rendered frames, which increases your frame rate. This does come at the cost of latency, but in a turn-based game like Star Wars Zero Company, that really doesn’t matter that much. Turn it on if you want a smoother image.

Nvidia Reflex/AMD Anti-Lag/XeSS LL: This setting will change depending on your GPU vendor but the underlying technology is similar across the board. These zero out your rendering queue, which lowers latency by only rendering frames as your CPU delivers them to your graphics card. Turn it on, there’s no reason not to.

Shadow Quality: If you’re GPU bound and struggling to get frames, Shadows are generally the first thing I cut. This will change how accurate shadows are, and even on low, they look halfway decent here (again, Unreal has a problem with scalability). Mid-Range PC: High, Handheld: Low

Global Illumination: This changes the quality of indirect lighting. This is another setting that mostly just affects your graphics card, so lower it if you’re GPU bound and looking for better performance. But if your graphics card isn’t even sitting at 100% utilization most of the time, this probably isn’t what’s causing your performance woes. Keep in mind though, that the High and Ultra settings here are using ray tracing, so going from medium to high will hit your GPU hard. Mid-Range PC: Medium; Handheld: Low

Reflections: Just like with GI, reflections are mostly a GPU-bound thing and Bit Reactor is using ray tracing here too. Just by virtue of this being a science-fiction game, there are a lot of reflective surfaces, so this can be pretty impactful to your performance, especially on a weaker GPU. Unless you have a high-end card, I’d keep this at medium. Mid-Range PC: Medium; Handheld: Low

Post Processing: I have a love-hate relationship with post-processing effects, and I’m not super happy that Bit Reactor rolled all of them into one setting. This will change everything from motion blur to bloom. This honestly won’t affect your performance that much, but if you hate motion blur, it might be worth turning this down just to save yourself a headache. Mid-Range PC: Your Choice; Handheld: Your Choice

Textures: This changes the resolution that textures are rendered at. This will mostly hit VRAM, so adjust accordingly. My tip would be to have a performance monitor up during one mission to see how much VRAM you’re using, and only lower this if you’re at the upper limit. Or, just turn it on Ultra if you have 10GB or more, and turn it to medium or low if you have less than 8GB.

Effect Quality: This will change how detailed visual effects are. This will affect everything from explosions to debris to lasers shooting through the sky. This is something that will hit your CPU, so if you’re being bottlenecked there, this is one of the settings you should cut. Mid-Range PC: High; Handheld: Low

Shading Quality: In this game, shading quality is essentially the same as mesh quality. It’ll change how detailed objects in the world are. Just like with textures, this is something I’d lower if you’re running out of VRAM. Mid-Range PC: High; Handheld: Low

View Distance: This is kind of a funny setting to even have in this game. This just changes how far out you can see details on objects from. But because of how small most of the arenas are, this is purely an aesthetic choice, and so I’m obliged to turn this down before most of the other settings. Mid-Range PC: Medium; Handheld: Low

Hidden Objects Detail: This changes how detailed objects that are currently hidden are. This will hit your CPU, so it’s something you should turn down if you are bottlenecked. Mid-Range PC: Simplified; Handheld: Simplified

Environment Geometry Detail: This is just a toggle that’ll change the geometry of models in the scene. Bit Reactor’s tooltip claims that newer GPUs won’t really see a performance benefit from turning it off, so I’d just leave it on unless you have an older PC – think more than 5years old. Mid-range PC: On; Handheld: Off

Jackie Thomas is the Hardware and Buying Guides Editor at IGN and the PC components queen. You can follow her @Jackiecobra

articles.title: Leaker Posts Extended Gameplay From GTA 6 Prologue Just Hours After Rockstar Warns Fans to Expect Story Spoilers
articles.summary: Extended gameplay footage revealing Grand Theft Auto 6's story prologue has been posted online, in a significant escalation of the past week's continued leaks.
articles.body:
Extended gameplay footage revealing Grand Theft Auto 6's story prologue has been posted online, in a significant escalation of the past week's continued leaks.

More than four minutes of gameplay featuring GTA 6 character Lucia is now being spread over social media, in the first lengthy leak of footage that reveals key story details. If you are planning to try and experience GTA 6 with no narrative spoilers, now is the time to beware where you click online over the coming days and weeks.

The footage's release comes just hours after Rockstar finally broke its silence over the leaks , which it called "heartbreaking" for its development team. In its statement, published online earlier today, the developer warned fans that spoilers would likely impact the manner in which it had hoped players would first experience the game — something that now appears to accurate.

GTA 6 Vintage Vice City Pack Screenshots

A fresh statement from the leaker, included as a watermark in this latest footage, makes several unsubtantiated claims about GTA 6's development, such as the game still being unfinished and that there was "too much" work left on the game to comfortably complete it before the title's November 19 release date.

Earlier today, Rockstar noted that it was indeed still working on the game — something that is fully to be expected with nearly three months left to go until launch — but that it was now "nearly" finished. The company also reiterated GTA 6's November 19 launch date, suggesting confidence that nothing would change.

The leaker has also claimed to have a "recent" build of the game, something that is again impossible to verify. However, there is now little doubt that these leaks stem from a polished playable build. Exactly how the leaker has gained access to it remains a mystery, but one which Rockstar and GTA publisher Take-Two are actively taking steps to ascertain .

Finally, the leaker once again called for "support" in the form of their own cryptocurrency, something that has been widely seen as a money-making exercise . Perhaps signalling that their leaking days may be winding down, the leaker suggested that "trading volume/price" of the $Cyberleek currency would determine whether the posting of footage will continue.

The past week has seen more than a dozen gameplay clips appear online , causing significant damage from a Rockstar perspective as numerous sections of GTA 6's world have now been revealed. According to Bloomberg , Rockstar has been left scrambling to discover how these leaks happened and who is behind them, as they have continued now for the past week.

Former Rockstar Games technical director Obbe Vermeij, however, has downplayed the damage caused by the leaks . Vermeij, who worked at Rockstar North from 1995 to 2009, took to social media to say that the company has weathered worse in the past, such as the Hot Coffee scandal.

Tom Phillips is IGN's News Editor. You can reach Tom at tom_phillips@ign.com or find him on Bluesky @tomphillipseg.bsky.social
