articles.title: Every LEGO Game on the Nintendo Switch and Switch 2 in 2026
articles.summary: Every LEGO game released for the Nintendo Switch between 2017 and 2026, from original LEGO worlds to collaborations with Fortnite.
articles.body:
The collaborative relationship between LEGO and Nintendo, two world leaders in family-friendly entertainment that operate in the adjacent realms of toys and games, began with the 1999 release of LEGO Racers on N64. At least one LEGO game has been released on a Nintendo platform nearly every year since, and multiple Nintendo-themed LEGO sets have been released each year since they debuted in 2020.

The LEGO-Nintendo synergy has persisted through the Switch era, and with the Switch 2 now out in the wild, we’re looking back on the legacy of LEGO on the Switch.

How Many LEGO Games Are Playable on Nintendo Switch 2?

As of 2026, 19 LEGO games have been released on Switch consoles , from LEGO Undercover City in 2017 to the most recent game, LEGO Batman: Legacy of the Dark Knight, in 2026. Of the 20 games, nine are LEGO originals and 11 are licensed collaborations with other intellectual properties.

Every LEGO Game on Switch and Switch 2 (Ordered by Release Date)

In April 2017, one month after the console’s launch, the series’ first game to hit the Switch was LEGO City Undercover , which is an original LEGO game originally released for Wii U in 2013. It’s based on the LEGO City series of themed building sets and tells the tale of an undercover police officer tracking an escaped prisoner.

LEGO Worlds is another original game released on the Switch in 2017. Worlds is the most authentically LEGO game available on Switch; it steps out of the series’ usual action-adventure genre into the world of sandbox games (think Minecraft), allowing you to build structures and environments brick by brick.

The LEGO Ninjago Movie Video Game (2017)

The LEGO Ninjago Movie Video Game is, as its name makes clear, an adaptation of The LEGO Ninjago Movie. The game and movie, both based on LEGO’s own Ninjago line , were released in the U.S. on September 22, 2017. The action-adventure game features eight locations and several playable characters from the movie.

LEGO Marvel Super Heroes draws characters and locations from Marvel movies and comics alike, with a massive roster of characters that (probably) includes every Marvel hero and villain you can think of. It’s a direct sequel to LEGO Marvel Super Heroes that ultimately pits you against the time-travelling villain Kang the Conqueror.

The first game is also available on the Switch, though you’ll find it further down this list – it wasn’t ported until 2021.

Another LEGO-Disney collaboration , LEGO The Incredibles combines story beats from both movies, the 2004 original and 2018 sequel. The game was released alongside The Incredibles 2 in June 2018. It features over 100 playable characters, including all five members of the Parr family. This game is one of many Disney games currently available on the Switch in 2025.

LEGO DC Super-Villains is a LEGO Batman spinoff focused on a collection of villains from the deep history of DC Comics, including The Joker and Lex Luthor. The villains must navigate the internal threat of personality conflict while pursuing the mysterious Justice Syndicate. It’s notably the first LEGO game to center its story around a player-created character.

The LEGO Harry Potter Collection is a compilation of two games: LEGO Harry Potter Years 1-4 and LEGO Harry Potter Years 5-7 . The collection includes the complete LEGO Harry Potter experience, pulling characters, stories, and activities from all seven books and eight movies . This collaboration goes hand-in-hand with the many LEGO Harry Potter sets that have released over the last few years.

The LEGO Movie 2 Videogame is a movie tie-in that was largely knocked for its lack of originality and innovation. The game blends elements of traditional action-adventure LEGO games with the building elements introduced in LEGO Worlds.

Originally released alongside the movie in 2015, LEGO Jurassic World came to Switch four years later in 2019. It features a 20-level campaign with five levels from each movie that had been released up until that point in time (Jurassic Park 1-3 and Jurassic World). In addition to characters from the Jurassic World movies , you can unlock playable versions of the franchise’s primary directors, Steven Spielberg and Colin Trevorrow.

LEGO Builder’s Journey came to Switch in 2021 after debuting on Apple Arcade in 2019. While most LEGO games incorporate puzzle-solving, Builder’s Journey is all puzzles, all the time. It’s a beautifully designed game that tells its father-son story one geometric puzzle at a time.

First released in 2013, LEGO Marvel Superheroes didn’t come to Switch until 2021. It tells an original story with several of Marvel’s most recognizable heroes – Spider-Man, Iron Man, Hulk, Wolverine, Captain America, and others – teaming up to foil the apocalyptic plans of Doctor Doom and Loki.

LEGO Star Wars: The Skywalker Saga (2022)

The definitive LEGO Star Wars experience, The Skywalker Saga features reimagined scenes from all nine Skywalker movies: the original trilogy, prequel trilogy, and sequel trilogy. Within this sprawling collection are over 300 playable characters, 23 planets, and 100 vehicles. Compared to past LEGO games, The Skywalker Saga moves you closer to the action by shifting the camera from a zoomed-out third-person perspective to a tighter over-the-shoulder view. Considering the sheer amount of Star Wars LEGO sets out there, it's no surprise this made for one of the best Star Wars games of all time .

LEGO Brawls is the worst-reviewed game on this list, based on Metascore (46). It’s an accessible, Smash Bros.-inspired fighting game originally released for Apple Arcade in 2019. Brawls features well over 100 minifigures/fighters from over 10 LEGO sets, including Ninjago and Jurassic World.

LEGO Bricktales is an original, puzzle-based adventure similar to LEGO Builder’s Journey, though on a larger scale. The game takes you to dioramas set in jungles, deserts, cities, medieval castles, and tropical islands. Bricktales was made by ClockStone Studio, the developer best known for its Bridge Constructor series.

LEGO 2K Drive , from prolific sports game developer Visual Concepts, is a racing game set in the open world of Bricklandia. 2K Drive is a robust racing game that features street, off-road, and water races; story, single race, tournament, minigame, and free-roam modes; and a custom car-builder that our review called “excellent.”

LEGO Fortnite is a collection of LEGO-themed games housed within Fortnite. Epic Games and the LEGO Group have created several LEGO Fornite experiences since the collaboration was launched in late 2023. Among the current ways to play are a survival-crafting game called Odyssey, an online social RPG called Brick Life , and a level designer called LEGO Islands.

LEGO Horizon Adventures was a collaboration between PlayStation’s Guerrilla Games and English support studio Studio Gobo. It’s a retelling of Horizon Zero Dawn, simplified and sanitized for a wider audience, that leans into the combat and platforming mechanics of LEGO action games before it.

LEGO Voyagers is a two-player co-op adventure that's short and sweet. In our 8 out of 10 review , IGN praised its meorable puzzle games and fantasticly presented world. It doesn't have the same level of depth as co-op games like Split Fiction, or It Takes Two, but it's a fun game you can play together with someone.

The second LEGO game we got in 2025, LEGO Party is, as you might guess, a party game along the lines of Mario Party. IGN's 8/10 review describes it as "Creative, colourful, and a consistent crack up... purpose-built to turn any boring old night into a block party filled with belly laughs." It feaures 60 minigames across LEGO sets from the Ninjago , Pirates, and Space themes. You can also customize your own minifigure and tackle Challenge Zones with up to three friends.

LEGO Batman: Legacy of the Dark Knight (2026)

We have officially entered the Switch 2 era, and this release happens to only be playable on the newer Nintendo console (as well as PC, Xbox Series X|S, and PS5). If you've seen any gameplay , you'll quickly understand why.

In the words of our reviewer , Simon Cardy, LEGO Batman: Legacy of the Dark Knight is a "lovingly made, often hilarious take on both Batman’s movie and video game history alike," with a particularly impressive take on an open-world Gotham. Unsurprisingly, the game was accompanied by a new spread of LEGO Batman sets .

Paradox Interactive just announced LEGO Skylines at gamescom 2026 . The game pretty much looks like a LEGO version of the studio's iconic Cities: Skylines city-building game, which sounds pretty freakin' awesome. There's no word on a release date yet, but we do know the game will be launching on Xbox Series X|S, PS5, Nintendo Switch 2, and PC.

Otherwise, there continues to be an endless list of upcoming LEGO sets . A series of live-action LEGO movies are theoretically in development, while most existing LEGO movies are available to stream online .

Jordan covers games, shows, and movies as a freelance writer for IGN.

articles.title: Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy Is a Prequel Spinoff That Takes a Lot of Interesting Chances With the Series, but Only Some of Its Experiments Pay Off
articles.summary: This prequel spinoff takes some interesting chances, only some of which pay off.
articles.body:
I tend to appreciate risky new ideas over safe sequels, so I was pretty interested to see what the Plague Tale series would be like without its signature tornadoes of man-eating rats. But while Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy makes plenty of intriguing changes, like its focus on a different protagonist and all-new cast of supporting characters, most cause it to fall short of capturing the same magic as its predecessors. This prequel story moves away from rat armies into more ancient, unexplored horrors that don’t live up to the high standards of the series, and its shift from stealthing around as a conflict-averse child to straight up knifing folks to death in melee combat never quite works when the fighting itself is too bare bones to sustain this 12-hour campaign. That said, the simple but entertaining puzzles, gorgeous environments, and tense stealth sections that eventually arrive later on are still mostly worth playing, but this side quest feels like it takes more steps backward than forwards overall.

Resonance follows the same third-person adventure playbook that you’re probably already familiar with. In the storied tradition of fellow “crevice crawlers” like Star Wars Jedi: Survivor or God of War, you’ll pass through a series of small combat arenas and puzzle rooms with a companion in tow as you banter with one another and the load-bearing story slowly unfolds. Most of this feels pretty similar to the previous Plague Tale games, with some pretty notable exceptions: Hugo and Amicia have been replaced with one of the supporting characters from A Plague Tale: Requiem, Sophia, and the stealth mechanics have mostly been swapped out for the typical third-person melee combat that’s common in these kinds of games. Unfortunately, like many of its peers, it also does that super annoying thing where characters immediately shout out the solutions to every single puzzle mere seconds after you step into a room – but thankfully there’s an option to turn that off, which I did immediately and with great prejudice.

While Resonance’s story is one of its strong suits, it’s still not quite on par with the rest of the Plague Tale series. What starts as an Uncharted-like treasure hunt devolves into a horrifying doomsday scenario that mirrors a lot of the same themes as Innocence and Requiem, but with a cast that gets significantly less care in how they are developed. It’s like they were trying to speedrun through the backstory for Sophia, who was a fairly flat character in Requiem. There, she was a generic outsider with a heart of gold who doesn’t have much of an arc, so Resonance had quite a bit of heavy lifting to do while fleshing her out. It succeeds only modestly on that front – I definitely knew her better and cared about her more after experiencing her harrowing tale firsthand, but also found myself perplexed by the fact that she still doesn’t have a real character arc, beginning and ending as the same scallywag in pursuit of treasure. That feels a little wrong with the lifetime of trauma I just piloted her through.

Instead, the ancient history you uncover actually pays off far more than Sophia’s personal journey. The bits and pieces that are revealed through flashbacks unravel the mystery of the long-dead civilization that’s at the center of her treasure hunt, and the characters, twists, and dialogue in these sequences drew me in far more than the hunt itself. By the end, it almost felt like Sophia was just a sidekick along for the ride (like she was in Requiem) rather than the focus.

The side characters have many of the same issues as Sophia, like Leni, the luck-obsessed pickpocket who tags along but never has anything interesting to say, or Faro, the captain of your pirate crew whose only likable trait is how much of a complete knucklehead he is at every leg of the journey. Despite spending a pretty good chunk of time solving puzzles and chatting with these folks, they never grew on me as much as I’d hoped, even if Faro’s hilariously terrible haircut did make me laugh every time I saw it. That really highlighted how crucially important the relationship between Hugo and Amicia has been in the other Plague Tale games, and this cast doesn’t fill the void all that effectively. They’re not bad per se, but don’t leave nearly as strong of an impression as I’ve come to expect from games that are as focused on the story as this.

The biggest difference with this prequel spinoff is that instead of creeping around armored enemies you have no chance harming, you’ll be standing your ground with a sword in hand, parrying and dodging about the battlefield and taking out enemies in simple, repetitive encounters. The shift from stealth to all-out combat isn’t the most seamless transition – not exactly bad, but consistently shallow and sometimes sloppy, with standard light and heavy attacks, a kick to break your opponent’s guard, and just a handful of bad guys with two or three different attacks to learn. So much of the time between its entertaining puzzles is spent in these claustrophobic arenas, but there’s so little depth to combat that it almost immediately felt too one-note to sustain my interest. I mostly just wanted to get these humdrum encounters done with as quickly as possible to get back to the story and puzzles that are a substantial step above.

You at least have a skill tree you’ll occasionally be able to buy a new perk in, which do things like give you a more powerful kick that knocks people back or gain temporary protection from damage after killing enemies. But these are mostly modest upgrades that help combat go by a little faster without making it any more entertaining. Hilariously, every once in a while Resonance will introduce a new mechanic to shake up the action, like glowing red attacks you can’t parry, only to then offer skill tree upgrades that make it so you can just… parry those red attacks, functionally removing that new mechanic so combat stays overly straightforward.

In between combat, you’ll have a welcome break from fighting as you solve the kinds of light-manipulating puzzles for which the series has always been known. These are easily the most enjoyable part of the adventure, though many of them are super simple light reflecting puzzles where you’re moving mirrors around to point a beam at a door. I’ve probably played about a hundred games with puzzles exactly like this, and while I don’t need Resonance to break a ton of new ground here, they do feel like a bit of a step backward compared to the clever ways the other Plague Tale games asked me to clear my path of rat hordes. That said, when the puzzles do hit, which is maybe half the time, it can be a lot of fun to snoop around old places and piece together clues from an old journal like something out of Indiana Jones.

Thankfully, these high points become more frequent later on, when the horrors of the rats are finally replaced by a new kind of danger. I won’t spoil it for you here, but certain sections return to the type of enemy you’ve no hope of facing head-on, forcing you to get creative in escaping it. You fight this new problem by, you guessed it, reflecting light into dark areas, so some of the puzzles are the same kind of unoriginal stuff you were already doing – but because the stakes are so much higher and the process of outsmarting the enemy is so much more exciting than simply opening a door, these sections immediately feel interesting and original in the way most encounters lacks for a large chunk of the story. This sort of stuff is what the Plague Tale games have always done best, and introducing a new kind of thing to be terrified of is pretty awesome, even if you do have to deal with the significantly less exciting combat encounters that continue to happen in between.

articles.title: 6 indie.io Games Coming to gamescom and PAX West That Have Free Demos on Steam
articles.body:
Publishing platform indie.io will be on hand at gamescom and PAX West in the coming weeks, and it’s bringing six games for people to try out in person. But if you’re not one of the lucky people who can be there yourself, don’t worry: all six games have free demos you can play on Steam right now, no badge or ticket required.

As tends to be the case with indie.io, their selection of games covers a wide range of genres. There’s everything from a cozy vineyard château builder to a brutal turn-based roguelite RPG. There’s a little something for all kinds of gamers, and you can try out all of them right now.

If you watched IGN’s recent Indie Loop showcase, you would have seen this game under another name. Formerly called Monster Zoo Tycoon, it unveiled its new name on August 10, but the dev team and core gameplay remain the same. In Monster Park Tycoon from developer OverPowered Team, you build and manage a monster park where visitors can come see a variety of strange and terrifying abominations. But there’s a twist: your park is a front for a cult. Not a very smart cult, at that.

In order to expand your park, you’ll need to trick and capture your guests using traps disguised as park props. Once you’ve got them, you can either feed them to your monsters, brainwash them to turn them into cultists, or sacrifice them to gain Faith and unlock favors from your Dark Lord.

Different monsters require different diets (like brains, blood, or souls), conditions for their exhibits, and behaviors that can become an issue if you ignore them. As your number of monsters grows, it’s inevitable that some of them will break free of their confinement, which is when all hell breaks loose. So you’ll have to control the chaos as you try to grow both your park and your cult in this darkly funny management sim.

Monster Park Tycoon has a brand-new demo available on Steam that marks the first time anyone outside the dev team has been able to play it.

In this roguelite, you’ll engage in tactical turn-based combat as you try to lead a band of survivors across a perilous desert in search of a new home. Your ship is fragile and your access to an all-important resource called Elios is limited. As you travel across the dunes, you’ll gather Elios from quests, from the bodies of defeated enemies, or if things get truly desperate, from sacrificing your crew members.

This is a roguelite, so you’re expected to fail. A lot. But each run builds on the ones before it. Each time a caravan is destroyed, you’ll start again with a new one. But you can find the wreck of the previous caravan, which can reward you with modules to empower your crew or even survivors who were part of your previous run.

Your crew has a roster of 15 classes with 16 unique traits that determine their skills, stats, and abilities. Combat takes place on a grid, where cover is available but the terrain is fully destructible. So you can mold that terrain to your advantage and use it to outwit your enemies.

Dunebound Tactics was featured during Steam Next Fest, and afterward its demo was rebuilt based on player feedback. In developer Terahard Ltd.’s own words, “If you haven’t played the demo recently, it’s not the demo you remember.” You can play the new and improved demo on Steam .

Quite a tonal departure from the first two entries on this list, We Took That Trip from developer Lucito Loquito is a calm and relaxing road trip game. There are no timers or deadlines, no great quest that needs to be completed. It’s just you and your cat traveling in a van and meeting new people.

There are three game modes to choose from: Story, Zen, and Background. Story Mode tells a heartwarming tale of friendship, loss, and reunion. Zen is just about the vibe, going for a ride with no real goal in mind. And Background is an AFK mode that takes care of the driving for you, so you can just enjoy the visuals and lo-fi soundtrack.

Each trip is procedurally generated and lasts as long as you choose, so every trip is different. There are points of interest scattered across your route, like gas stations, stores, and lookout towers, where you’ll meet people and hear their stories. But the focus is always the road and your Microbus, which you customize both the interior and exterior of with paint, stickers, and other decorations.

If you’re looking for a peaceful way to de-stress after a long day, you can check out the demo on Steam .

The peaceful vibes continue with the aptly named Cozy Builder, a sandbox building sim from Pangea Game Studios where you’ll start from scratch and restore Vineyard Valley to its former glory. You’ll use modular architectural pieces to create your château and harvest grapes, herbs, and wildflowers to create your own wines and other goods to share with the townsfolk or sell to continue funding your château.

There are tons of customization options for your château, including a variety of artwork and furniture for the interior and gardens, terraces, and greenhouses for the exterior. You can connect the greenhouse to your home, giving you a place to nurture flowers and collect rare plants.

You can do all of this solo or build a shared space with your friends in multiplayer, giving each of you the chance to show off your creativity. The demo has been getting updated throughout the summer to add new features, like one-click item moving in destruct mode and full key rebinding. You can try it out for yourself on Steam .

This open-world survival crafting game from developer Pequi Studios sees you wake up alone on an island after a mysterious crash. You’re injured, disoriented, and surrounded by untamed wilderness, so you’ll have to find a way to sustain yourself and survive. To do that, you’ll need to gather resources, craft tools, hunt wild animals, catch fish, grow crops, and build a homestead that can sustain you while you try to figure out what happened to you.

As it turns out, the island you washed up on is one of 24 that make up an archipelago, and your adventure will take you to all of them, each of which has different environments, resources, and hidden treasures. So you’ll need to continuously upgrade your tools and figure out how to adapt to each island’s challenges.

There aren’t any timed objectives or linear paths, so you decide the pace at which the story unfolds. If you want to spend hours building up your base, raising animals, and tending crops, you can do that. Or you can just find what you need to keep surviving and move on to the next part of the story, it’s up to you.

That story of Mayday: The Survival Island is focused on the mysteries of the island and how you ended up there. You’ll find strange symbols, magical totems, and fragments of a lost civilization that hint these islands are more than meets the eye. And the more you explore, the more you’ll question if ending up here was an accident and if escape is even possible. You can get a taste of all this with the free Steam demo .

The last game on the list is the only one that’s already had its full release, but you can still play a free demo on Steam . Esports Manager 2026 from developer Neurona Games released in July and had a successful launch, peaking at more than 10,000 concurrent players and landing on Steam’s Popular New Games list.

The game is exactly what the title says: a management sim where you control the day-to-day operation of an esports organization. You’ll scout players, sign staff, manage contracts, develop talent, grow your brand, and lead your team in tournaments against the best of the best. You can take over an existing organization or build your own from scratch, and you can recruit and develop real esports players.

During tournaments, you’ll lead your team in Simulation Mode, where you control your team’s tactics and react to in-game events in real time. A major content update recently landed that rebuilds the loan system, reworks the maps in Simulation Mode, and allows retiring players to return as coaches and analysts.

The update was accompanied by a 25% discount that will last until September 8, so if you’re interested, now’s the time to try out the demo and see if it’s for you.

articles.title: I've Tried Star Wars Zero Company on Five Different PCs, and It's Been a Nightmare
articles.summary: Star Wars Zero Company is an incredible game, but it's marred by all kinds of technical issues on PC, particularly at the hands of Epic's Unreal Engine 5.
articles.body:
We got off to such a great start this year, with a ton of PC games that looked great and still ran well on pretty much any hardware. One of the common themes among games like Crimson Desert , Resident Evil Requiem, and Forza Horizon 6 was that none of them were running on Unreal Engine 5. And just like Halo: Campaign Evolved last month , Star Wars: Zero Company is a great example of why I'd love it if developers simply abandoned Epic's engine altogether.

I've spent about five hours in Zero Company so far, and while that means I'm still pretty early in the otherwise fantastic game, I've still run into more than my fair share of technical issues, across all types of hardware. When the game isn't bugging out in some way, I've been having a blast with it, and it's important to note that our reviewer Dan Stapleton hasn't had nearly the same depth of issues that I've had.

What's funny is that the technical problems are different on each of the systems I've tried the game on.

I was on vacation last week, so the first laptop I tried the game on was my Razer Blade 16 , with an RTX 5090 and a Ryzen AI 9 HX 370. It got a decent average frame rate at 1600p, but it was plagued with microstutters, especially in cutscenes. I started getting driver crashes, where the game would just make my laptop restart whenever I tried to load the game up — something that doesn't happen with any other game right now.

I also spent some time playing the game on the Lenovo Legion Go 2 , which I've installed Bazzite on. Anyone that's ever tried to play an Unreal Engine 5 game on a handheld probably won't be surprised, but it didn't run super well. In order to get a playable frame rate, I had to lower the resolution to 800p with the lowest settings, and I was still only getting about 25–30fps. But that by itself isn't necessarily a deal breaker with this type of game. It's turn based, so I can absolutely live with a 30fps experience here.

For some reason, the game loves to crash right at the end of a mission. The system will lock up, forcing me to do a hard restart, and lose all my progress. This happened a good four times before I just gave up. That one likely comes down to Linux. I had a similar problem on the Steam Machine, where the game would crash on the same level, only the Steam Machine actually gave me an error report that I could send to the developer.

Once I got home a couple of days ago, I had to see what would happen on a top-end rig with an AMD Ryzen 7 9850X3D , 32GB of RAM ,and an RTX 5090. The performance, even with that level of hardware, wasn't great . I was only getting 70–80fps at 4K with Ultra settings with DLSS set to Quality and frame generation disabled. That's still very playable, mind you, but halfway through my first mission on that desktop, the game just froze in the middle of a turn.

Bit Reactor has already come out with a day-zero patch that fixes some problems, but even after installing it, I continue to run into crashes, freezes, and frame drops constantly. I have to imagine that the game will get to a more stable point eventually, and I'm looking forward to it. After all, Zero Company, along with Galactic Racer have been two of my most anticipated games this year.

I'm going to keep trudging along with Zero Company despite all my trials and tribulations with it. There's just something about the prequel era of Star Wars that just ensnares me, and the story definitely has its hooks in me. I just wish sitting down and playing the game wasn't such a recipe for headaches right now. Maybe some day.

Jackie Thomas is the Senior Tech Editor at IGN and the PC components queen. You can follow her @Jackiecobra

articles.title: Resonance A Plague Tale Legacy Review, Gameplay Impressions, Videos and Top Features
articles.summary: Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy from developer Asobo Studio means to evolve, both in fleshing out its world and characters, and in terms of gameplay experiences it offers to players.
articles.body:
Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy from developer Asobo Studio means to evolve, both in fleshing out its world and characters, and in terms of gameplay experiences it offers to players.

A sequel to 2022's A Plague Tale: Requiem and third overall in the series, Legacy steers away from the stealth roots of the series and leans into the action side of things more.

No longer so grim and tense, this bold direction takes A Plague Tale closer to a Tomb Raider or even Uncharted territory while finding a narrative goldmine in a fan-favorite side character, pushing her into the protagonist's limelight.

New Grand Theft Auto game leaks confirmed

The result is a close-to-home-yet fresh experience that feels as much a homage to those other series as it does a unique Plague Tale effort, which is a nice balance to strike.

Plague Tale games have easily been some of the best-looking games of their respective generations.

There's a visual treat around every corner here, whether it's sunny tropical environments with lush fauna or seedy temples with lethal risks on every surface. The realistic visuals and stunning sound design, in soundtrack or otherwise, creates a deep level of immersion.

If there's a complaint, it's that some of the animations can look goofy at times, especially when running, crouch-walking or within some of the transitions during combat. However, this isn't a deal-breaker at all.

As a more action-oriented experience, the expected gameplay staples emerge in terms of parrying, counters and finishers.

Sophia wields a sword and dagger as primary weapons and they deal bonus damage in certain scenarios and with proper timings. There's also the option to weave in kicks and, in a fun twist, her grappling hook.

It all feels really good , especially the parries and counterattacks. Tops among everything, though, is how pretty shockingly realistic enemies react when knocked into each other or the environment. There's angle and environment-specific finishing moves, too. No game but the recent James Bond effort has come close to this sort of next-generation-feeling action that actually loops in the things around the players.

Not bad for what was, until now, a primarily stealth series, right?

Puzzles, another strength of the series, don't get as much of a glow-up. There's the expected stuff, like dodging spike traps, shifting light sources, scanning around for secret ink and the like. But a chunk of it can feel like a tempo-breaking pitstop in what is very much an action-oriented tale.

Not necessarily a bad thing, as there are only so many ways these games can evolve on the puzzles played decades ago in Nathan Drake games.

It's a fun effort and enjoyable enough to explore, especially when it all comes together with good environmental storytelling and engaging combat done better than most in terms of interactions with the world around the fight.

Set 15 years before Requiem, players take on the role of Sophia.

Sophia was, of course, a hit character in Requiem for her enthralling personality and actions while players visited her ship. Now, in prequel action, Sophia is younger, more brash and, unlike the last time players saw her, more than happy to do some killing along the way in her adventures.

Frankly, phrases like emotionally exhausting weren't uncommon around the first two entries in the series. Tonally, it makes sense for the series to step back and take more of a lighthearted, almost swashbuckling feel to the world. A younger Sophia and the narrative here make it successful.

Kudos, too, to the decision to go Uncharted-like with Sophia's notebook. She sketches out gorgeous prints of an area that can sort of take the place of a traditional video game waypoint marker.

Beyond the strong narrative, exploration gets rewarded with goodies to find. Progress is as expected, in a good way, and there are some solid tutorials to bring players up to speed with the game's systems. Points earned can be spent on new skills and upgrades, that sort of thing.

Along with a strong suite of settings, accessibility and otherwise, Legacy offers five different difficulties aimed at appealing to all audiences.

As a sort of spinoff game in a beloved series, Legacy is a big hit. As an action game, it doesn't tread shocking new ground that will repave the genre for those that follow.

Even so, similar to the visuals and immersion provided by the two prior games, Legacy is a treat for those reasons and its next-gen-feeling combat, choppy animations notwithstanding.

Undoubtedly, there will be those who bemoan the brief series departure from the depressing, supernatural rat horror stuff. But Sophia is an endearing character who drives the narrative in fun directions and absolutely accomplishes the goal of fleshing out the Plague Tale world in interesting ways.

articles.title: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4's Beta Will Be Playable on Switch 2 for Free This Weekend
articles.summary: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 will be playable on Nintendo Switch 2 for free this weekend.
articles.body:
Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 will be playable on Nintendo Switch 2 for free this weekend.

Starting Friday, August 28 at 10 AM PDT, Nintendo Switch 2 players will have the opportunity to try Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 for free. The beta's second weekend will kick off, giving Nintendo fans the opportunity to try a level from the game's campaign, multiplayer, and even the battle royale, Warzone.

The Switch 2 version will boast unique features such as gyro controls, Joy-Con mouse controls, and, of course, being able to play the game on a handheld. Additionally, Switch 2 players will get free access to the game's Vault Edition content during the beta. This includes access to special skins, weapon blueprints, and more. Players can pre-load the beta on Switch 2 right now and pre-order the full game.

It's the first time a Call of Duty game has been on a Nintendo platform since Call of Duty: Ghosts on Wii U. Nintendo fans have been wanting to see the franchise return to Nintendo hardware since then, but it hasn't been feasible until now. Digital Legends are developing the game's Switch 2 version after having helped develop Call of Duty: Warzone Mobile before its cancelation. The studio also did support work on the last two Black Ops games.

"For the first time in more than a decade, Call of Duty is back on a Nintendo platform, and we’re incredibly proud that Digital Legends has partnered with Infinity Ward to make it happen with Modern Warfare 4, said Xavier Carrillo-Costa, studio head, Digital Legends. "Our goal has been simple from day one: deliver the genuine Call of Duty experience on Nintendo Switch 2. Players can enjoy the full intensity, authenticity, and quality of Modern Warfare 4 wherever they are, whether at home or on the move."

In 2023, Microsoft signed a legally binding deal with Nintendo to bring Call of Duty games to Nintendo platforms for a decade with full feature parity. That means there's no missing content or notable concessions made to bring Call of Duty to Switch 2. Whether Nintendo fans show up for this release remains to be seen, but it's great to see Switch 2 being supported more and more by the biggest third-party franchises out there.

For a very limited time, the biggest and baddest gaming monitor you can possibly get (short of getting a TV) has dropped to its lowest price ever. Samsung via its official store is offering the massive 57" Samsung Odyssey Neo G9 Dual 4K UHD gaming monitor for $1,349.99 with free shipping. If you click on the link and you see $1,449.99, don't give up! All you have to do is reload the page about three to five times. This discounted price is reserved for "select" customers, but Samsung is essentially just RNG-ing it every time someone lands on the page. Once you see that, add the $50 off upgrade credit on the product page, and then apply 10% off coupon code " L8AS4HAL4O " in your shopping cart. Your final price will be $1,170 . This monitor retailed for $2,500 when it first launched in late 2023.

Reload this page until you see the price of $1,349.99 (usually 3x to 5x refreshes)

At your cart, apply 10% off code "L8AS4HAL4O"

Final price will be $1,170 with free shipping (before taxes)

The 57" Samsung Odyssey Neo G9 is one of few 57" dual 4K UHD monitors on the market, boasting an eye-watering 7680x2160 resolution, or the equivalent of two 4K UHD monitors stacked next to each other. Despite the display being so large, it has an above-average 140ppi pixel density, which is amazing considering the fact that in general the bigger the display, the lower the ppi. To put that into perspective, it's as sharp as a 32" 4K monitor. Wow.

The Odyssey Neo G9 is equipped with a Mini LED backlight paired with a quantum dot (QLED) panel. Like its namesake suggests, mini-LED panels have smaller LEDs than traditional LED LCD monitors, so you can squeeze in more lighting zones. Mini-LED monitors are also much brighter than OLED monitors, which is very important because larger monitors are generally dimmer than smaller ones to start. Local dimming combined with higher brightness improves contrast ratio and HDR and is also useful in overpowering glare and reflections.

The Samsung Neo G9 isn't a one-trick pony, and all the other specs live up to what we'd expect from a top-end gaming monitor. The display boasts an aggressive 1000R curve that practically hugs you as you play games. Curved panels are useless with small monitors but extremely helpful with super-wide ones. It also features a 1ms response time and 240Hz refresh rate. It is HDR1000 certified, which means that it can maintain peak brightness up to 1,000 nits. It's FreeSync Premium Pro certified , which means it works with G-Sync in compatibility mode as well.

Should you buy the Samsung Odyssey Neo G9 ?

Obviously, the Samsung Odyssey Neo G9 isn't a monitor for everyone . You need a rather generous gaming budget. Also, not all games support this resolution and aspect ratio. Some games will have letterboxing to compensate. Finally, gaming at dual 4K UHD resolution is extremely GPU intensive. Make sure you have a good graphics card that can handle the load. We'd recommend something no less powerful than a GeForce RTX 5070 Ti or Radeon RX 9070 XT.

articles.title: How Midnight Spider-Man Transforms Peter Parker Into a Terrifying Monster
articles.summary: Marvel's horror-themed Midnight Universe is one of the most exciting new developments in comics this year, and we've got the full scoop on Midnight Spider-Man from writer Phillip Kennedy Johnson.
articles.body:
Alternate comic book universes are all the rage lately, with both Marvel's Ultimate Universe and DC's Absolute Universe consistently topping the sales charts. The only problem for Marvel is that they just ended the Ultimate line this summer . Where do they go from here? How do they continue that momentum? The answer, it seems, is to shift focus to another brand-new universe, but this time focused on infusing classic Marvel properties with elements of horror.

The result is the Midnight Universe, a new imprint set in a twisted version of the Marvel U where iconic characters have been given drastic makeovers. One of the three pillars of that line is Phillip Kennedy Johnson and ScieTronc's Midnight Spider-Man. What happens when your friendly neighborhood hero is given a full-fledged body horror makeover? To find out, we spoke with Johnson via email. Check out an exclusive preview of the first issue in the slideshow gallery below, and then read on to learn more about the new series and how it delivers a profoundly different take on Marvel's most popular hero:

To start off, we were curious about the mission statement of the Midnight Universe. How does this project compare to something like the Ultimate line? Is it still about letting creators take big swings in a way that aren't possible in the mainline Marvel Universe continuity?

"On that initial meeting with the three writers, senior editorial, and Marvel President Dan Buckley, the quote from Dan I remember most clearly was 'horror in the front seat, superhero very much in the back,'” Johnson tells IGN. "I took that as permission to go as hard as we want to go. I’m approaching it like a creator-owned horror series, honoring the core of the Spider-Man story but retold as a prestige horror title. And not 'horror' just in its horrifying imagery, but hopefully also in its concept, atmosphere, and thematic relevance that makes all the best horror stories hit as hard as they do.

When the Midnight Universe was announced, there was some initial online pushback from fans who expected the line to focus on classic supernatural characters like Blade and the Midnight Sons. Which begs the question - was there talk of focusing on more traditional horror characters? Does Johnson feel like reinterpreting these iconic heroes is actually the more potent approach in this case?

"Marvel’s traditionally supernatural characters have come up in conversation, and I have no doubt they’ll show up in our stories at some point," Johnson says. "But the focus for the launch was always Marvel’s most classic, iconic characters. When the initial teaser for Midnight went up, EVERYONE who saw it assumed the same kind of imminent follow-up announcements: Midnight Suns, Blade, Werewolf by Night, Moon Knight, Tomb of Dracula. Everyone thought they knew what was coming, there wasn’t even a discussion."

Johnson continues, "That was exactly the reaction I was hoping for, and to me, it confirmed that we were doing the right thing in embracing the unexpected. Midnight isn’t just a sticker on the cover of all our business-as-usual horror titles. It’s a complete reimagining of the entire Marvel Universe. If we launched the Midnight Universe with a Blade title, the risk is that “Midnight Blade” would look an awful lot like the Blade of the 616 Universe. Midnight Blade wouldn’t give us anything new, that’s what he’s always been."

With the Ultimate Universe, creators were pretty much left free to tell their stories within the framework of the two-year real-time format Jonathan Hickman established, with those characters finally converging when the line reached its climax in Ultimate Endgame. What is the approach to the Midnight Universe? Is Johnson focused on telling his own story, or are Midnight Spider-Man, Hickman and Matteo Della Fonte's Midnight X-Men, and Benjamin Percy and Kev Walker's Midnight Fantastic Four building to a larger, overarching story?

"Right now we’re all focused on making each individual story as great as it can be, but there’s a lot of discussion between us as we go," Johnson says. "One of the biggest perks of this gig is that Jonathan, Ben and I talk or text nearly every day about the books. I was a fan of both those guys long before we started working together, and it’s a privilege to see their scripts and get to know their processes. We all keep track of where the other two are in our stories, we offer up our scripts and art for feedback, we keep each other posted on story elements that might be of use in the other titles. It’s a proper writer’s room, and it’s a joy to be a part of.

Reinventing Spider-Man for the Midnight Universe

One of the most obvious ways in which Midnight Spider-Man reinvents the mythos involves the radioactive spider itself. This isn't another case of Peter suffering a tiny spider bite and transforming overnight into a superhuman. This is a long, painful, drawn-out transformation, and the book's body horror elements are reflected in the fact that we see this oversized arachnid fused to his chest. So how much is that transformation and its psychological effects a focus of Kennedy's early issues?

"I need to be careful not to spoil what the iconic spider is, and what it’s doing to Peter… it’s a mystery we’ll slowly reveal over the course of the series," Johnson teases. "I want people to have their own theories, and for those theories to escalate and evolve as we slowly reveal what’s happening to Peter. But I can say the body horror escalation from issue to issue is extreme. The hope is that by the time our readers read issue #3, they’ll be hard-pressed to imagine where it can even go from there. We’ve had to get very creative with the fringe science of the story to ensure there are still horrific new vistas to explore 25, 50, and 100+ issues from now. Every time an issue hits shelves, I want our readers sweating and shivering all the way until the next one hits."

The prospect of a body horror-centric take on Spider-Man is certainly intriguing. We were curious if there any particular influences from film or comics/manga that Johnson and ScieTronc are drawing upon.

"Within film, the biggest influences on the series are probably the films of David Cronenberg, John Carpenter, and Guillermo Del Toro," Johnson says. "Del Toro influences everything I do, though… he’s one of my favorite storytellers in any medium. And I’ll add H.R. Giger to that list. Even though he’s not technically known as a filmmaker, there’s no Alien without Giger. His work blurs the lines between biology, technology, sexuality, and the most horrific body horror, and his work will inspire the imagery of Midnight Spider-Man all the way to the end.

As for comics, Johnson says, "Many of the biggest influences are horror manga, or horror/action: primarily the work of the great Junji Ito, but also Homunculus, Parasyte, Chainsaw Man, and others. Within Western comics, eagle-eyed readers will see some influence from the Garcia/Rubin Beowulf adaptation, which I think is a work of genius. Bendis’ and Oeming’s Powers. I’m also being mindful of DC’s and Marvel’s 'universe reimaginings' that have come before: Bendis’ Ultimate Spider-Man and New Avengers, Hickman’s more recent Ultimate Spider-Man, Absolute Batman, Wonder Woman, others. What we’re doing in the Midnight Universe is very different from any of that, but they were all executed so well, there are a lot of lessons to be learned from them as we find our way in the Midnight Universe."

Johnson adds, "Also: this might be a strange thing to say, but ScieTronc’s art has probably been the biggest influence on my writing for Midnight Spider-Man. His art completely shapes the way I write for him. The manga influence on ScieTronc’s work is obvious at a glance: it has all the facial expressiveness and dynamic action that manga does so well, but there’s also a super high level of detail, rendering, environmental interest, and creative layout that the best Western comics have. If I was writing for any other artist, the story would be completely different. I've had to educate myself in some ways to make sure I'm giving him scripts that best honor his style and skill."

While Peter Parker's enduring feud with Norman Osborn has always been a hallmark of the franchise, Midnight Spider-Man seems to widen that scope and double down on the conflict between this lone vigilante and the billionaire oligarch class. The series is certainly wading into topical waters, but how does Midnight Spider-Man redefine the theme of power and responsibility for 2026?

"The mission statement of Spider-Man has always been 'With Great Power there must also come great responsibility.'" Johnson says. "But writing Spider-Man in 2026—MIDNIGHT Spider-Man in particular—we have to acknowledge that the world we live in has almost completely refuted that premise. A much truer statement in 2026 would be: POWER MAKES MONSTERS."

Johnson continues, "Midnight Spider-Man is the collision of those two tenets. Peter Parker is a brilliant but frustrated kid yearning for personal transformation, who NEEDS 'Power with Responsibility' to be true, and he lives his life in such a way to prove it. And against all odds, he gets his shot at power and greatness… but just like the rest of the powerful, his power changes him in horrific, monstrous ways. Throughout the series he denies it, he fights against it, he desperately tries to cling to his humanity even as it slips further and further away. We’ll spend the entire series answering the question of which version of Peter wins in the end."

Midnight Spider-Man #1, Midnight X-Men #1, and Midnight Fantastic Four #1 wll all be released on October 7, 2026. You can preorder them at your local comic shop .

articles.title: The Division 2: Echoes of Central Park Announced
articles.summary: Massive Entertainment, developers of Tom Clancy's The Division 2, announced a new DLC for the long-running online action-RPG/third-person shooter at a community panel at Gamescom. The new expansion is called Echoes of Central Park, and a full reveal will happen on September 24.
articles.body:
Massive Entertainment, developers of Tom Clancy's The Division 2, announced a new DLC for the long-running online action-RPG/third-person shooter at a community panel at Gamescom. The new expansion is called Echoes of Central Park, and a full reveal will happen on September 24.

The Manhattan-set live-service game will finally head into Central Park due to a distress call from inside it. Echoes promises a darker tone wrapped in fear and mystery, with neither players nor their in-game avatars sure about what's inside or what Central Park has been like since the outbreak.

Massive promises ample replayability for this DLC, including "a few twists" to give gameplay a unique feel. Speaking of gameplay, the developerse also want to lean heavier into gameplay here, rather than just new story content. Exactly how that will manifest itself remains to be seen.

IGN gave The Division 2 an 8.5 out of 10 back in 2019 and the 2020 DLC Warlords of New York an 8 out of 10 .
